newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Airlines plan seen missing mark.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Airlines plan seen missing mark.

text.p: Canadian Airlines Corp.'s survival plan unveiled last Friday falls short of addressing the ailing carrier's domestic overcapacity, seen as its major cash drain, some observers say.

Canadian's management said the plan, which would see a reduction in domestic traffic, a boost in U.S. and Asian capacity and a 10 percent wage cut for employees, was necessary to keep the airline aloft.

"While much of the rhetoric is concentrated on Canadian focusing on Asia, in reality, it is not so, and that is why the company is continuously short of cash," Research Capital Corp. airline analyst Jacques Kavafian wrote in a report on Monday.
"It is trying to become another Air Canada, but there is obviously no room for another such carrier in the country."
Canadian, which has not posted an annual profit this decade, said on Friday that the plan aims at bolstering its bottom line by C$800 million ($600 million) in the next four years.
It said it faced a cash deficiency in the first quarter of 1997 if its harsh initiatives were not accepted by unionized employees and 33 percent-owner AMR Corp. by the end of November.

Canadian's biggest unions, the 5,300-member International Association of Machinists and the 3,700-member Canadian Auto Workers, said after the announcement that they were not prepared to take another round of wage rollbacks.

Ted Larkin, analyst with Bunting Warburg, said the company's management, led by Chief Executive Kevin Benson, faced a daunting task in convincing the various forces to come on side within the tight deadline.
"The fuse is short on this thing and it calls for some rather drastic measures to be taken," Larkin said.
The domestic operations in Canada's airline sector creak under the weight of too much capacity, a situation aggravated by the entrance this year of no-frills discount carriers.
Under the Canadian survival strategy, the carrier plans to use smaller aircraft on many of its domestic routes and cut others, freeing up Boeing 737 jets to fly transborder service.
The move is part of a plan to double service from such U.S. cities as Las Vegas, Boston, Dallas, Chicago and Portland, Ore., hoping passengers connect at Vancouver for flights to Asia.

Analysts said other new routes would likely include flights to major U.S. hubs such as Dallas, Miami and Chicago, from Vancouver, Calgary and Toronto, which are currently flown by partner AMR Corp.'s American Airlines.

But Kavafian said holding on to such routes as Toronto-New York, Toronto-Chicago and Toronto-Ottawa did nothing for Asian operations because there was little connecting business to the Pacific Rim from those points.
Employee wages, however, are not seen as the big factor behind financial turbulence at Canadian.
"It's only part of the story but it's not the cause of the problem," said Larkin. "The big problem has been the fact that there's too much capacity domestically chasing far too few travelers."

For the short term, Kavafian urged investors to avoid Canadian stock, saying it risked a steeper decline even at today's levels. "The situation right now is one of survival, not stock appreciation," he said.

Canadian shares on Monday were down C28 cents (21 cents) to C$1.33 ($1). Air Canada, reaping the benefits of Canadian's troubles, gained C50 cents (38 cents) to C$5.85 ($4.39) in heavy trade of 1.9 million shares.
